name: Wilhelm Ambrosius Eisenheart

backstory.title: A Life of Science
paragraphs: Raised by his single mother, Elise Bleckburn, a beloved innkeeper at the edge of the Shrouded District, after his father abandoned her, Wil Bleckburn was a loved but often lonely child. His mother caught Ater-Lung Disease, a fatal (hereditary) disease infecting a person’s lungs with slowly festering cysts, corroding the soft tissue and resulting in a slow almost inevitable death. His mother passed when he was eight years old. An event bearing a mark on the young boy’s later years.

Thankfully he was taken in by one of the Spired District’s many orphanages and shortly after adopted by house Eisenheart, a noble family with great investment in scientific progress, providing generous donations to the Scions and even being rumoured to have financially supported the Obitus Scholare in the past. He was renamed Wilhelm Ambrosius Eisenheart, a name more befitting of a noble son.

At age 14, he was allowed to join the Scions, learning under some of the best weaponsmiths and engineers. A gifted young mind, much to his adoptive parents’ delight, he quickly fit in with the brilliant minds found within the Scions’ ranks. As his final thesis, the final step of becoming a proper Scion, he had to present his studies findings, once he reached the age of seventeen. His creation, weapon-enhancements made from the bones the Scions had acquired, combined with iron, meticulously forged into a rare alloy, capable of redirecting and controlling lightning, soon brought him great attention within scientific circles. Bleckglass was created.

With 19, Wil developed the first symptoms of Ater-Lung, prompting him to join the Mortis Engineers, a brand new branch of Scions emerging during the early years of the First War, hoping to maybe someday return those claimed by death. Wil however was uninterested in reviving the long gone, seeking to instead find a way to survive the disease that had ended his mother’s life before him. Two years of rigorous uncompromising research followed, research that cost several innocent lives. In the meantime, Wilhelm’s health gradually declined, death almost claiming him several times, before he could hope to archive the impossible.

In the end, it was the alloy he had created, Bleckglass, which proved to be the key to success. Its unique properties when in contact with lightning, he found, were the key to reviving those lost. Just in time, as Wilhelm’s last breath grew imminent,  his experiments grew closer to completion. His revivification, although not flawless – his heart laid silent, he could no longer enjoy food nor drink – was his greatest success. His countless attempts of recreation failed. Despite this, his work yielded different impressive results.

Those dying on the frontlines could be brought back, if only for a few minutes at a time, before the strong currents of electricity burned through the cold flesh, to fight a little longer, to strike fear into the enemy and to prove Luyarnha would not fall this easily. Bleckglass, though hard to come by – and even harder to maintain without the knowledge it required – no way to produce more and time having scattered the alloy across Luyarnha’s streets, is highly sought after by knowledgeable Scions, most of which Mortis Engineers.

backstory.title: In Search of Hope - 7 AGK
paragraphs: Wilhelm pulled the lever with enough force to break it, desperation and adrenaline clutching at every fibre of his mind, body and soul. Pain rattled his chest, making it harder to breathe, agony striking like lightning, causing an awful cough to sting in the back of his throat. He fought for air, trying desperately to calm his racing heart and shallow, futile breathing. Yet, all attempts failed, as his hand missed the table by a hair’s width, and he toppled to the floor, arms wrapped around himself, blood trailing from his lip.

He could not stand the pain. Every fibre of his body screamed at him to somehow make it stop. He did not want to die. Not yet. He needed more time. He deserved more time. He had hardly lived at all! Why could he not have more time? Was it too much to ask?

If the Church would not help, or maybe their faith was truly not worth what they claimed, if Carmella could not find a cure, if the sciences, which he had dedicated his life to, did not have an answer for his plight, then he would simply do it alone. Wilhelm pulled himself up from the ground, hand clutching the desk above, and dragged his tools towards him. When he reached for the Bleckglass cores, another cough forced his hand to halt. This time, it did not bring him to his knees. His fingers curled tightly around the shards of alloy.
It needed more testing, he knew. It needed more time. But that was something he did not have. He could not afford to delay. Time was running through his fingers like water.

No known flame burned hot enough to melt Bleckglass, so Wilhelm did not worry, as he heated the shard, until it shone bright white. The last one needed, he hoped. His hands and wrists, his collarbone, ankles and spine held such shards already, burnt – ingrained – into flesh and bone. Ozzhark had almost refused him, when he had begged for his help with the one set in his spine.

Gritting his teeth, he brought the shard up to his face, inspecting it. Bleckglass smelt of ozone and sulfur dioxide, when heated, not unlike lit gunpowder, but exponentially more pungent, almost suffocating. Before the alloy could grow too cold, he brought the metal to right beneath his chin, where his jawbones ended. Breathing out, his lungs burning, as if suffocated by the simple action, he grasped his jaw tightly, covering his mouth and forcing the back of his head to the wall, ensuring his reflexes would not ruin him.

The second that glowing hot point of metal touched his skin, he jabbed his hand upward. With no air left in his lungs to scream and biting down on his own hand, to distract – if only for half a second – Wil sunk to his knees again. His heart stuttered, when his fingers found his pulse. He felt dizzy, unable to tell left from right, up from down. Once more – maybe for the last time – he forced himself up and stumbled towards the metal stretcher in the room’s centre.
A Bleckglass lightning rod readjusted, a metal wire forced back into place, lights flickering, then turning off. A final lever to pull. He reached up, fingers locking weakly around the metal.

Wilhelm’s hand slipped, the feeling in his arms entirely gone. His heart had stopped. Breathing felt impossible, and futile. All his work for nothing? He would take his very last breath, so close to archiving the impossible? One more attempt.
And the world went black.

backstory.title: Day of the Dead Arisen - 10 AGK
paragraphs: (Suggested Song: RISE)
The news of the frontline reached the Scions late. Almost too late. Almost.

“Trust me, Ozzhark. If all goes according to plan, the people of Luyarnha will never again doubt us. This will strike fear into the hearts of the Southerners. This will ensure Luyarnha’s victory!” Wilhelm argued, gesturing towards the high window of the estate, overlooking the Spired District, vaguely pointing towards the frontline outside the wall.

“You are oddly convinced of this plan, Wilhelm, are you sure there is no personal motivation beyond our image?” The Orc narrowed his eyes, holding Wilhelm’s gaze through the younger’s crimson coloured glasses. They could not fool one another. Of course Wilhelm had further reason for his action. Teodor was out there, trapped by the Southern forces having breached the lines of defence. His battalion was stationed in the trenches beyond the wall, surrounded by the enemy, doomed to die, if nothing or nobody intervened. The Jaegers could not reach them, and without the soldiers having their backs, the living weapons could not tear down the invaders besieging the city. The darkest day for Luyarnha, since the Jaeger’s creation.

They remained for a few moments longer, gaze locked in silent debate. Finally, Ozzhark sighed, lowering his head. “If this fails, it shall be on you. You will take the fall.” Wilhelm nodded once, then turned to cease wasting further time.

The Mortis Engineers were not known for cowardice. Every one of them would do what it takes. Every one of them agreed to Wilhelm’s plan. Friedrich had offered his help immediately upon hearing about the planned strike. And they had sent word to the front, shortly after receiving the go-ahead.

Their force was small, as they set out, hidden by the dark veil of night. The Jaegers stationed on top of the walls watched the group of Scions gather curiously. They had promised forces to back them. None of which could be seen yet. Wilhelm could hear their whispers, see their distrust. What would scientists be able to do in war?

“We have yet to test this, do you truly believe this will work?”, Lune locked him down with a fierce glare. She was sure of their limits, careful in her approaches, observant, brilliant, but held back by her ceaseless worrying. Although, for once, he could not disagree. The risks were immense, potentially even devastating to them. Raising a corpse was difficult, intricate work. Too little and it did not stir, too much and it turned to dust. The power needed for his plan to succeed was beyond what was measurable. Wielded carelessly it could kill all of them. But he was not going to let that happen. Nor was he about to stand down.

“I do. Focus on channelling the lightning we need, let me handle the rest.” He looked out beyond the wall. The Southerners’ camp was dimly illuminated by a few specks of light, dimmed lanterns to prevent proper pinpointing of their position. The trenches dug between them and the wall were wide, reeking of dread and death, a vital part blocked by advancing enemy forces, trapping their own out there.
The illusionist with them, a young hunter, shrouded the group in darkness, as they descended. (Suggested Song: The Attack of the Dead Men and/or Stormtroopers)

Immediately, the Engineers went to work. One hundred Bleckglass lightning rods. Every single one in existence met the field today. Twenty-three Mortis Engineers to control them, not enough to exert proper control, not enough to ensure a fail-safe plan. “You said they will follow their last command”, Friedrich watched him critically, as Wilhelm forced a Bleckglass rod into a corpse’s cranium. He dearly hoped one would be enough to raise the body, if only for a shortened duration. “Yes. Defend Luyarnha, drive back the enemy.” “I hope this works.”

The sun rose from behind the horizon, covering the sky in deep dark red, as black lightning struck. Momentarily, his allies followed Wilhelm’s lead, raising the bodies around them from their eternal sleep. And with one hundred dead arisen, they advanced. A deafening boom split the air. The Southerners had seen them. Shortly after, all hell broke loose. Arrows descended upon them, soldiers were felled. However, for every corpse fallen, a new one arose. The Mortis Engineers stuck to the back, vigilant as to who they revived, careful to stay out of harm’s way and keep their marionettes moving. The Jaegers had joined the fight, jumping in to take out one enemy after the other.

The enemy, struck with fear, seeing the dead rise from the trenches, and the living weapons descend on them like devils fresh from hell, moved chaotically, some disregarding orders, others pushing through fear and doubt but falling against the charged strikes of the undead. In the midst of chaos and warfare, Teodor was shouting commands to his troop, who joined the fight valiantly. After only a handful of seconds, that felt like lifetimes, he spotted Wilhelm commanding his undead, formerly fallen brethren. The warrior paused, if only briefly, shocked by the revelation, but no less elated to see his friend.

Wilhelm felt light-headed. The lightning he called and channelled struck through his veins like venom, static coursing through him in lieu of blood. If his heart were not unbeating, it would have stopped certainly. Which was exactly why he had insisted on leading their undead forces. He was moving through the crowd of fighters quickly, trying not to slip on mud and blood. He slid to the ground next to the disintegrated remains of a Luyarnhian soldier, drawing the lightning rod, burning hot – normally their temperature remained cool to the touch, no matter the voltage, he noted, worriedly – grasping it firmly between bloodied fingers and forcing it through the eye of another fallen next to him. With a jolt of lightning, the corpse rose, immediately defending him from an incoming attack. The young Scion tasted metal. When he raised his hand to wipe his mouth, it came away deep red, doused in warm blood from his nose. Gritting his teeth, he pushed back up, dodging away from the fighting. Lightning was dancing across the battlefield, spreading like a web all around them. The power they were using for this was immense, but Wilhelm was certain every last bit of it was worth it. His vision refused to clear, the world drifting in and out of focus periodically. A world normally tinged in black and red slowly dulled, as if all colour was drained from it, leaving but black and white. And yet, he pushed forward.

Friedrich caught up with him, taking him by the arm. The weapon expert and skilled fighter looked him over, once, before shouting commands to the surrounding force. When lightning began to cease, Friedrich called for proper retreat. The Jaegers complied. Teodor’s battalion, still driving back the incoming force, now turned to retreat to safety. (Suggested Song: As We Fall)

The lieutenant himself was the last to retreat. And although Friedrich tried pulling his fellow Scion along, the older slowed down to await his friend catching up. The revived around them slowly crumbled to dust and ashes, urging all allies to hasten their step.

Wilhelm turned, spotting Teodor not far from him, twisting out of Friedrich’s grip to join his side. But before he got the chance to, something moved behind the warrior. And before either of them could react, Teodor’s blood covered the already stained grounds, his steps faltering upon the spear piercing through his back. A Jaegar jumped to meet the blade of the attacking Southerner, but Wilhelm hardly had the mind to care about the enemy’s proximity. Focus locked upon his injured – dying – friend, he dropped to his knees next to him, frantically reaching for the Bleckglass rod at his side.
Friedrich stopped behind him, shocked gaze locked upon the frightening display of a sharp lightning rod, sparkling with electricity, being struck between the commander’s ribs.

Teodor awoke to the sickening taste of blood and pain surging through his body in waves. The pungent smell of ozone surrounded him, mixed with old blood and mud, he was all too familiar with. He felt like throwing up. He might have, if his body had enough strength to move at all. But in the end, he could not even open his eyes. For but a moment, he felt a familiar presence at his side, someone helping him up, before he drifted back into unconsciousness.
(Suggested Song: Resurface and/or Heart Heart Head)

“What happened?” He had awoken to people moving, talking, working. On a bed, comforting and warm, so unlike the wet dirt he had thought might become his final resting place. Slowly, he had recognised his surroundings as the medical wing within the Cathedral. His memory was blurred. Every time he tried to remember, he felt nauseous, nothing coming back to him, no matter how hard he tried. “Apparently, you were killed.” A young man, the blood-red Innarda, symbol of the Blood Cross, displayed proudly on his armband, explained carefully. “None of us were dispatched on the stakeout to retrieve your troop, therefore I can only repeat what we were told by the Hunters, who had joined your side.”

Teodor had almost stopped listening, only briefly looking up, worry-stricken, “My troop. Did they make it?” The young man paused. Blinked. Then smiled. “Yes. They counted no casualties resulting from the retreat. I’m still uncertain, whether to believe what the Militia claims. The dead brought back to life, back to fight. But then again, they claim you died too. And yet, you arrived here, still breathing, your heart still beating.” He looked toward the window, a few thin streaks of light falling through the glass, fracturing into different colours. “They say the South is going to retreat. Luyarnha reigned victorious in our last strikes against them.” Eyes wide, Teodor stared up at him. Last he remembered things were looking up, until they were caught unawares, trapped outside the wall. With the Jaegers it was no wonder they- “Wait. How long was I unconscious?”

Three weeks. Three weeks and no sign of Teodor’s recovery. Slowly, Wilhelm had started believing he would never see his friend again. The effort – the pain – for nothing. Only to be left with a hollowness inside, that he was all too familiar with. One that was more painful than the days immediately following the rescue, more painful than dying to corroding lungs.

Agonisingly slowly he made his way to the laboratories. The crutch under his arm still holding most of his weight, as his body refused to recover faster. He had overdone it. Horrifically so. He could hardly walk, worse, he could not work at all in this state. He had passed out once already, trying to handle the faintest current.

When they had returned from the front, after Teodor and the other injured were taken to the Cathedral, Wilhelm had almost fainted on the spot. Friedrich had mentioned being struck by a painful jolt of lightning, when he had tried supporting him on the way back. He did not recall making it back home at all.

Wilhelm’s notes on the matter, although slightly chaotic, painted a fairly clear picture on why they should never attempt something like that again. A worthwhile lesson in self-preservation, he supposed. Hearing people speak of that day positively left a bitter taste in his mouth, one of metal and bleach. Hearing them call it ‘Day of the Dead Arisen’ felt almost like a celebration. A sentiment he could not share, until he knew for certain Teodor was alive. Until he knew it had not been for nothing. No amount of success would weigh against that hole in his heart.

Further down the hall, the young paladin, having been discharged by the Blood Cross’ healers a mere hour ago, was looking at the countless books propped up neatly on top of the shelves lining the walls. He had wanted to wait in the laboratories, but a Scion he was not sure he knew – she had introduced herself as Lune – had advised against it. Instead she had told him to remain in the foyer outside said rooms.

When he heard feint steps, accompanied by a slow, rhythmic thud, Teodor looked up. He could not help but smile, seeing Wilhelm walk in, immediately crossing the distance between them and pulling the engineer into a firm, yet gentle, hug. Wil looked up at him then, with wide, sparkling eyes – eyes filled with so much relief, so much joy – tears threatening to fall from his lashes and that small, almost invisible smile he wore so well. “You look like you walked through hell.” He smiled, feeling sadness tug at the corners of his heart. The younger man’s eyes were brimmed with red, deep circles underneath them, starkly contrasting the deathly pallor, worse than usual even, of his skin. He was cold to the touch and Teodor could tell, if he were to let go of him now, the scientist would crumple like a marionette, whose strings had been cut. And yet, Wil merely smiled, hand resting over his heart as if to make sure it was still beating.

“You were dead”, he breathed after a long moment of silence. One that Wilhelm had spent counting the slightly hastened beats of Teodor’s heart, listening to his slightly uneven breaths, feeling the warmth of his hand covering his own. “I thought, for a moment-” “Yet I’m here. Thanks to you.” They remained like that for several long moments, Teodor keeping him upright, holding onto him, like he was something fragile, something precious. And finally, Wilhelm realised, he felt like all that work, all that pain, was worth it.

backstory.title: Of Slow Dances and Swift Mistakes - 11 AGK
paragraphs: (Suggested Songs: Shatter Me (Secret Garden))

Wilhelm stood leaned against one of the walls, watching finely dressed nobles move around the room, like perfect figurines in masterfully crafted music boxes. The war was won. And of course, noble houses had no better way to celebrate, than to host grand masques, invite to feasts and dance to flaunt their riches. Pretending all was well, despite the lower classes starving, despite them having to bear the aftermath of the war, of the losses. He felt sick at the thought.

Across the room he spotted Leopold and Alida talking with a young man the Scion could not help but recognise. He had not thought Teodor would be here tonight. A noble couple joined the small group, catching the elders’ attention. Wilhelm could guess they were expressing their condolences regarding Ignaz. It was not fair. The war had already been won that day. And yet, his brother was not here to see the ballroom dressed in blue – the new colour of victory, after yellow became tainted with the memory of the Godless King. He was fully aware, if it had been up to his parents, Ignaz would be standing here, instead of their false son, who could only watch a room doused in grey.

Wilhelm turned, picking up his walking aid, still unable to function without it – unable to take part in the celebration, to at least try and appease the heads of House Eisenheart – he could not even explain what had happened. The church had twisted the narrative around the Day of the Dead Arisen – as people still insisted to call it – for their own benefit. So now he had been injured in an experiment gone awry. The thought appalled him more than he would care to admit.

The halls of the Eisenheart estate were exactly as hollow, as he remembered. The walls lined with fine décor, shelves filled with items and books none of the children of the family had ever been allowed to touch, high windows revealing starry skies. A crescent moon dimly illuminated the streets of the Sanctified District, hiding the despair of the people, hiding the monsters roaming the same streets, while cloaked in shadow. When he finally reached the library, his legs were shaking. Faint music still filled the air. He closed his eyes to listen, once he found a seat upon one of the windowsills.
(Suggested Songs: Can You Hold Me, In This Shirt, (War of Hearts))

Maybe he should have stayed away. He had work to drown himself in, rather than being suffocated by people he did not fit in with. And with his body still broken by his own actions, he could not even begin to pretend. The doors to the library opened, immediately causing the engineer to turn towards it and freeze in surprise. “Teodor? What are you doing here?” “I could ask you the same. I do not believe I have ever seen you pass up on a chance to dance?”, his eyes followed Wilhem’s, as they fell upon the crutch. He all but winced. He stepped closer, despite Wil forcing his gaze out the window, unwilling to look at him. The paladin, in turn, watched him curiously. Then he sighed. “I never quite thanked you for what you did, have I?”

Hearing this, Wilhelm raised his gaze to lock eyes with him. A rare sight, when he was not wearing his glasses. Teodor could not help but hold his gaze. Maybe a little too long. Then, he offered a hand. “May I ask for this dance?” The younger man’s eyes flickered to his hand, then back to meet his gaze, confusion evident on his elegant features, visibly trying to decipher Teodor’s thoughts. Admittedly, the latter could not decipher his own. After a long moment he feared he might decline. Just as he was about to withdraw his hand, Wilhelm hesitantly took it. Teodor pulled him up onto his unsteady feet, one hand coming to rest at his side to support him. Wilhelm could not help but stare at him, watching his every move in an attempt to figure him out. And yet failing to. “I can barely stand and you want me to dance with you?”, he queried finally. Instead of answering, Teodor merely adjusted his hold on him, one hand on his waist, guiding Wilhelm’s own to his shoulder, before interlocking their hands. His grip firm but gentle, the paladin only smiled. “Simply lean on me.” The younger man blinked. He felt hot all of a sudden, having to avert his gaze to calm his racing thoughts. Were his heart still beating, he was certain, it would have jumped out of his chest.

And to the faint music reaching them from all the way down the hallways, they danced. Slowly moving through the room, much like they would on the ballroom floor. “Thank you.” When Teodor spoke, Wilhelm looked up, holding his warm gaze. “For saving all of us out there. For saving my life.” He guided their interlocked hands to his chest, as if to show him how his heart still beat. The Scion stumbled slightly, the unexpected shift in balance catching him off guard, but Teodor held onto him, saving him from falling and drawing him closer to himself.

Wilhelm looked at him then. Silvery white eyes studying his face carefully, uncertainly. That same faint smell of ozone, like the sky after a horrible storm, accompanied by an acrid, singed smell, reminiscent of the powerful machinery the engineer worked with, that same smell he remembered from the battle, enveloped him. He remembered people complaining about it, saying it smelt noxious, dangerous. He could not agree with them. To him, static and ozone smelt of power, and of mystery. Teodor realised he was still holding Wilhelm close, still watching the tiniest flickers of uncertainty cross his friend’s face. With their hands between them, Teodor could feel the lack of a heartbeat, he took note of the unnaturally cold skin of his friend, of the scars along his jaw and hands and of the dark metal pierced through his ears and lower lip. His eyes caught on the latter. For a moment all he wanted was to lean in and close the last bit of distance between them, share his warmth with him, know him by his side. Then logic returned to him, reminding him how wrong that was. How nothing could ever exist between them. And just then, Wilhelm closed the gap between the two of them. He was hesitant, uncertain. But when Teodor pulled him closer, he could feel him smile.

Reality crashed upon him like a wave. When they separated, Teodor’s heart dropped. He could pretend to have kissed someone else, kissed Mina, kissed any woman, as long as his eyes had been closed. Wil wore his hair longer than most, wore unusual clothes. When he closed his eyes, Teodor could pretend. Looking at him now, he could no longer pretend. And he felt sick at the thought. It was plain wrong, he knew. His parents would never have approved of this. Besides, he was absolutely certain he did not like men. Wilhelm with his cursed slim waist and soft lips had caught him off guard, had ambushed him, enough to confuse him for but a moment. He had merely wanted to thank him for what he had done. He had not anticipated any of this happening. Stoically, he stepped away from him, all but dropping Wilhelm, who, now without support stumbled, barely managing to catch himself on the windowsill. Before he could say anything, Teodor turned, all but fleeing the room. Seeking him out had been a mistake.
Wilhelm was left alone, staring at the now closed door. After another moment, his strength left him, as he sank to the floor, tears burning behind his eyes. What had he done?!
Within the same week, he received a letter. The envelope bore the Sternfeld crest. An invitation. To Teodor and Mina’s marriage.

backstory.title: In Search of Connection - 11 AGK
paragraphs: Her Greenhouse looked almost exactly the same, almost untouched by the First War’s raging. Impossible to believe it was over. Impossible to believe they had won. Though it hardly felt like winning. Wilhelm looked up, eyes tracing the dark stone, lined with intricate carvings, gothic metal and rich flora weaved together so naturally, so perfectly. Much like the building’s mistress, it took one’s breath away. If he had still needed to breathe, that was.

The two Manikins followed on his heel, as the young Scion stepped through the gates. It had been four years, since he had last visited. Only a blink of an eye for an elf, like Carmella. For a moment he feared, she might have forgotten him. That he might not have left even a trace of an impression. Yet, when he left the vast doors behind him, and Carmella turned to see who might be seeking her out, all worry fell away. “Wil”, her smile, reserved for medical miracles and scientific breakthroughs, or so he had thought, was graceful as ever. “When I did not hear from you, I must admit, I feared the worst.” “A fault of mine I hope you may forgive”, he breathed a kiss to her hand, when she lifted it towards him. Her eyes sparkled. He could see the questions burning behind her eyes. Last time he visited, he had been dying after all. And yet, he stood before her. She rested her hand upon his chest, like she often did, when trying to console or comfort the ill seeking her help. “Never have I heard of Ater-Lung ceasing within the afflicted. Your survival-”, she halted, when she realised. His heart was not beating.

“What have you done?”, her eyes, now wide, sought his. Instead, they fell upon the line of metal, embedded deep within his skin and the scars around the wounds, still raw, even after years passed by. Carmella reached up, slowly, carefully, placing her hand along his jaw, guiding his gaze down to meet hers. Healing magic, warm and comforting, seeped through his veins, as her fingers gently traced along the scars. Pain he had believed would haunt him forever ebbed away. “The impossible. I dared face death and came away victorious.” He covered her hand with his. They stood, for a moment, neither moving, neither breaking the silence. She understood, he hoped. They both ventured far beyond the unknown in their studies, they shared the same impossible dream. A healer and a scientist, both hoping to one day archive immortality. If anyone would understand, it was her. Then she dropped her hand, briefly resting it upon his chest again. Waiting. Maybe for a heartbeat to return. It would not, Wilhelm knew. “Mostly.” He added, admitting to the failures within his own resurrection. She stepped back. For but a moment, he feared he had been wrong. Then. “Tell me everything.”

“So, this little thing saved your life?”, she inspected the Bleckglass lightning rod in her hands, holding it up against the light. Wilhelm watched her. He did not trust many with his work, but he lacked those qualms with her, at least to some degree. “How do you make it?” There it was, the inescapable question he always received. Normally he would wave people off, tell them they would not understand his work, even if he tried to explain it. “It’s quite a complicated process, really. A carefully balanced combination of glass and iron at its core-” “Glass? What would glass serve in a lightning rod?” He smiled. She always asked the right questions. “As I said, complicated.” Her gaze fell upon the Manikins, standing by the stairs. “Would you be interested in extending our trade deal?”, he raised an eyebrow. Allowing a Bleckglass core outside the influence of the Mortis Engineers, more pressingly, outside the hands of Scions? Could he take a risk like that? His eyes fell back upon Carmella, then upon her journal, which detailed all kinds of remedies. A faint smile played around his lips, as he sighed. “What is your proposal, dear friend?”

npcs.name: Lady Mina von Sternfeld – Half-Elf 66
npcs.description: Second daughter of the noble house of Sternfeld, a family deeply tied to the fine arts within Luyarnha, Mina was fostered by the Eisenheart family, a tradition commonly practised even beyond the city, after her fourteenth birthday. She and Wilhelm became great friends shortly after, two minds fitting together seamlessly. They were inseparable. Things grew more complicated, when Mina started catching feelings for Wil, around the same time he struggled with his disease rearing its head. He changed in those short years, grew distant, while she was left trying to pick up the pieces of the person she fell in love with. Life did not wait for either of them though. When Mina was pressured into marriage, Wilhelm refusing her, she had no choice but take a different man as her husband.

npcs.name: Lord Teodor von Sternfeld – Half-Elf 67
npcs.description: As the eldest son of the now fallen noble house of Renford, Teodor grew up with high expectations and suffocating responsibility resting on his broad shoulders. Due to old alliances, Teodor often visited the Eisenheart estate, becoming friends with Wilhelm and Mina. A talented fighter, since his earliest years, he fought for Luyarnha in the First War. Losing his left arm and just barely escaping death’s grasp, he was sent back to recover. Wilhelm designed and built his prosthesis, resulting in the two spending a lot of time together. He never dared say it out loud, but it was during that year Wil fell for his friend. Unfortunately Teodor had lost his heart to another. When he mentioned his feelings for Mina to the young Scion, Wilhelm had kept silent. Teodor returned to the frontlines and left the war as a seasoned, prestigious veteran and commander. Soon after, he asked for Mina’s hand in marriage and she accepted. Even today, he fights for what he believes in, standing strong against the Scourge.

various:
very punchable face (bit of an ass with very little filter, not a good combination) remarkably smart but equally pragmatic not afraid to pursue his ambitions, no matter the cost fiercely loyal, although he is mainly thinking of himself, once he cares about someone he will do anything for them

carries a strong scent of ozone – a sharp, pungent smell, stinging in the back of the throat – and metal, beneath this almost overwhelming odor, faint traces of, wet dirt? And yes, death, seem to cling to him
